Newly hatched zoea larvae of the Arctic lyre crab possess a dry weight of 0.0000318 grams , reflecting the limited endogenous reserves packaged into each offspring. The corresponding energy content at this initial stage is a modest 0.55 joules , a value that imposes tight constraints on the duration of the early planktonic phase. During the larval interval, individuals feed actively and accumulate biomass, and by the time of metamorphosis to the megalopa stage, the dry weight has increased substantially to 0.000261 grams . The energy content at metamorphosis, measured at 3.65 joules , represents an approximately seven-fold increase over the birth state, reflecting the trophic gains achieved during the zoeal instars. These developmental benchmarks align with general patterns observed among spider crabs of the family Oregoniidae, where a high ratio of metamorphic to birth energy reserves supports the morphological transformation and subsequent benthic recruitment.

Following settlement and metamorphosis, juveniles begin a protracted phase of somatic growth that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity. The timing of this developmental milestone has been investigated under controlled thermal conditions; at a stable water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the estimated time from settlement to the onset of puberty is approximately 300 days from settlement [tp = approximately 300 days from settlement]. However, some studies using field-reared individuals have reported a slightly longer interval of 365 days post-settlement [tp = 365 days post-settlement] at the same temperature, a discrepancy that may reflect variation in food availability or local density-dependent growth suppression. The carapace length at which females reach puberty is approximately 0.9 centimeters [Lp = approximately 0.9 centimeters], a dimension that corresponds to a wet weight estimated at 0.41 grams [Wwp = 0.41 grams]. This weight threshold indicates that females must achieve a critical body size before allocating resources toward egg production. Males, in contrast, tend to mature at a larger carapace length of 1.1 centimeters [Lp = 1.1 centimeters], with a corresponding wet weight at puberty for males of 0.72 grams [Wwp = 0.72 grams], a difference that likely reflects the energetic demands of male-male competition and the maintenance of larger chelipeds used in mating interactions.

Adult Arctic lyre crabs exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism in both body size and growth trajectory. The ultimate carapace length for males reaches 6.1 centimeters [Li = 6.1 centimeters], a value derived from growth-curve analysis of large, presumably senescent individuals captured during trawl surveys. This carapace length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 128 grams [Wwi = 128 grams], placing Hyas coarctatus among the larger-bodied members of its genus. Females typically attain smaller asymptotic sizes, although the allometric relationship between carapace length and body mass remains consistent across sexes. The maximum reproductive output of an adult female has been a subject of considerable interest, particularly in comparisons with the commercially important congener Chionoecetes opilio. Extrapolations based on relative fecundity suggest that, when maintained at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], an individual female produces approximately 3,250 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 3,250 eggs per clutch] and sustains approximately 0.0072 clutches per day [F_R_i = approximately 0.0072 clutches per day] over the course of the reproductive season. This daily egg production rate of approximately 23.4 eggs per day, sustained across the brooding period, requires substantial energetic investment and likely depends on the availability of high-quality benthic prey such as polychaetes and small mollusks.

Longevity estimates for the Arctic lyre crab remain somewhat provisional due to the difficulty of age determination in crustaceans without persistent calcified structures. Analyses of body size distributions and mark-recapture data have, however, provided an estimated maximum lifespan of 19 years [am = 19 years] when crabs are reared at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This value aligns closely with the maximum longevity reported for the snow crab Chionoecetes opilio, suggesting that the two species share a broadly similar pace of life under analogous thermal regimes. This relatively extended lifespan is accompanied by a delayed maturity, as the time from settlement to the attainment of sexual maturity, previously noted as 300 days from settlement [tp = 300 days from settlement] or 365 days post-settlement [tp = 365 days post-settlement] depending on the study population, is followed by a further period of growth before first reproduction occurs at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. The ultimate carapace length for males of 6.1 centimeters [Li = 6.1 centimeters] is typically reached only after many successive molts, each incrementally adding to the exoskeletal dimensions.

An integrated perspective on the life history of Hyas coarctatus reveals a strategy defined by moderate fecundity, relatively slow growth, and pronounced iteroparity. The daily egg production rate of approximately 23.4 eggs per day under a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] is sustained across multiple brooding cycles, but can be decomposed into a per-event fecundity of approximately 3,250 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 3,250 eggs per clutch] and a frequency of approximately 0.0072 clutches per day [F_R_i = approximately 0.0072 clutches per day], allowing females to spread reproductive effort over several years. The ultimate wet weight of 128 grams [Wwi = 128 grams] attained by the largest males represents an enormous increase from the 0.72 grams [Wwp = 0.72 grams] wet weight recorded at puberty for males, highlighting the magnitude of post-maturational somatic growth. This pattern of continued expansion after maturity is a hallmark of crustaceans with indeterminate growth, enabling them to increase reproductive output with age. The 19-year maximum lifespan (19 years) [am = 19 years] places this species among the longer-lived brachyurans, a trait that likely buffers populations against years of poor recruitment in the variable subarctic environments they inhabit at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Collectively, the energy content values at birth and metamorphosis, the sex-specific size thresholds for maturation, and the thermal dependence of development underscore a life history that is finely attuned to cold-water, food-limited benthic ecosystems.
